rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders al-hayawan as the only true life, contrasting the hereafter with worldly diversion and play.
rows.anchor: the life in the hereafter is indeed the only [true] life: if they but knew this!

none: translation only; no separate commentary point

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the earliest Qur'anic revelation to mention the term and concept of riba.
rows.anchor: This is the earliest mention of the term and concept of riba in the chronology of Qur'anic revelation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ordinary linguistic usage, riba means an addition or increase beyond a thing's original amount.
rows.anchor: In its general, linguistic sense, this term denotes an "addition" to or an "increase" of a thing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Qur'anic terminology, riba is an unlawful interest addition to money or goods lent by one person or group to another.
rows.anchor: in the terminology of the Qur'an, it signifies any unlawful addition, by way of interest, to a sum of money or goods lent

rows.speaker: most of the early Muslim jurists
rows.claim: Early jurists generally treated unlawful riba as profits from any interest-bearing loan, whatever the rate or economic motive.
rows.anchor: most of the early Muslim jurists identified this "unlawful addition" with profits obtained through any kind of interest-bearing loans

rows.speaker: Islamic scholars
rows.claim: Islamic scholars have not reached a comprehensive definition of riba that covers every legal case and changing economic need.
rows.anchor: Islamic scholars have not yet been able to reach an absolute agreement on the definition of riba

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathir
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir calls riba one of the most difficult topics for scholars.
rows.anchor: In the words of Ibn Kathir (in his commentary on 2:275), "the subject of riba is one

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The legal condemnation and prohibition in 2:275–281 was the Prophet's final revelation, received only days before his death.
rows.anchor: the passage condemning and prohibiting riba in legal terms (2:275-281) was the last revelation received by the Prophet, who died a few days later

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because this legal passage came at the end of the Prophet's life, the Companions had no chance to ask him about its legal implications.
rows.anchor: the Companions had no opportunity to ask him about the shar'i implications of the relevant injunction

rows.speaker: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab
rows.claim: Umar said the final revelation on riba was left unexplained by the Prophet; Asad cites Ibn Hanbal through Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.
rows.anchor: even 'Umar ibn al-Khattab is reliably reported to have said: "The last [of the Qur'an) that was revealed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran's severe condemnation, viewed alongside later economic experience, sufficiently shows riba's nature and social and moral effects.
rows.anchor: the severity with which the Qur'an condemns riba and those who practice it furnishes - especially when viewed against the background of mankind's economic experiences

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Riba's blame attaches to interest loans exploiting weaker borrowers: lenders retain ownership and guaranteed gain regardless of how funds are used or whether borrowers lose.
rows.anchor: the opprobrium of riba (in the sense in which this term is used in the Qur'an and in many sayings of the Prophet) attaches to profits

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Classifying transactions as riba is ultimately a moral question tied to the socioeconomic motives shaping the lender-borrower relationship.
rows.anchor: the question as to what kinds of financial transactions fall within the category of riba is, in the last resort, a moral one

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Economically, the issue is how borrowers and lenders can share profits and risks equitably.
rows.anchor: it is a question as to how profits and risks may be equitably shared by both partners to a loan transaction

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No fixed answer can cover all eras; successive generations must reinterpret riba as social, technological, and economic conditions change.
rows.anchor: our answers must necessarily vary in accordance with the changes to which man's social and technological development - and, thus, his economic environment - is subject

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although riba's condemnation is final and unequivocal, this early mention stops short of a clear legal prohibition and foreshadows the later ban through its condemnation of exploiting others' possessions.
rows.anchor: the Qur'anic condemnation of the concept and practice of riba is unequivocal and final, every successive Muslim generation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to 2:276 for a related statement about riba.

words: أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا۟ أَنَّا نَسُوقُ ٱلْمَآءَ إِلَى ٱلْأَرْضِ ٱلْجُرُزِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad makes the revival of barren land and its crops a sign pointing to resurrection.
rows.anchor: Can they not, then, see [the truth of resurrection]?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally means morning and evening but signifies all times.
rows.anchor: Lit., "at morn and evening", i.e., at all times.

none: translation only; no separate commentary point

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad connects David's special favor with the preceding elliptical reference to repentance and cites 38:24, where David recognizes his sin and repents.
rows.anchor: This connects with the elliptic reference to repentance in the preceding verse: David is singled out for special mention in view of the allusion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links the mountains and birds praising with David to the parallel passage at 21:79.
rows.anchor: Cf. 21:79 and the corresponding note 73.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hadid primarily means sharp, concretely or abstractly; Asad cites 50:22 and Arabic idioms for sharp intellect, bold sight, and a sharp odor.
rows.anchor: The term hadid denotes, primarily, something that is "sharp" in both the concrete and abstract senses of the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite form al-hadid may denote sharpness or iron; the latter allows a literal soft-iron rendering.
rows.anchor: An alternative rendering of the above phrase would be: "We caused iron to become soft for him"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads the softening of sharpness as an allusion to David's aesthetic sensibility in the Psalms, goodness, and humility.
rows.anchor: God's having "softened all sharpness" in David is evidently an allusion to his exalted sense of beauty (expressed in the poetry of his Psalms) as well as to his goodness and humility.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As an alternative, Asad allows a literal softening of iron, alluding to David's gifts as poet, warrior, and ruler.
rows.anchor: An alternative rendering of the above phrase would be: "We caused iron to become soft for him", which might be an allusion to his outstanding abilities as poet, warrior and ruler.

words: أَنِ ٱعْمَلْ سَٰبِغَٰتٍۢ وَقَدِّرْ فِى ٱلسَّرْدِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sabigh means ample, abundant, or complete; plural sabighat functions as a noun for abundant, perfect deeds, supported by the related verb asbagha at 31:20.
rows.anchor: The adjective sabigh (fem. sabighan) signifies anything that is "ample", "abundant" and "complete"

words: أَنِ ٱعْمَلْ سَٰبِغَٰتٍۢ وَقَدِّرْ فِى ٱلسَّرْدِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sard denotes a consecutive continuation, with parts or stages following steadily, continuing, or repeating.
rows.anchor: The noun sard, on the other hand, denotes something "carried on consecutively", or something the parts (or stages) whereof are "following one another steadily"

none: translation only; no separate commentary point

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement concerns Judgment Day and echoes 6:164, which also says each person's wrongdoing rests on that person alone.
rows.anchor: I.e., on Judgment Day - for "whatever [wrongj any human being commits rests upon him alone" (6:164

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads the first clause as denying the Christian doctrine of original sin burdening humanity.
rows.anchor: the first part of the above statement implies a negation of the Christian doctrine of "original sin" with which mankind is supposedly burdened

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads the second clause as categorically refuting the doctrine that Jesus vicariously atones for that sin.
rows.anchor: the second part categorically refutes the doctrine of the "vicarious atonement" of that sin by Jesus.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to 53:38 and the corresponding note as a parallel statement.
rows.anchor: See also 53 :38 and the corresponding note 31.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only those who believe in realities beyond human perception can benefit from the warning; Asad points to 2:3, 27:80–81, and 30:52–53.
rows.anchor: only those "who believe in the existence of that which is beyond the reach of human perception" can really benefit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses the living and dead as spiritually alive or dead, extending the metaphor to those described as lying in graves.
rows.anchor: the living and the dead [of heart]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad's translation glosses those endowed with knowledge as having innate knowledge and standing in awe of God.
rows.anchor: only such as are endowed with [innate] knowledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad connects the beauty of nature's varied colors with 16:13 as evidence of God's creative power.
rows.anchor: where the splendour of nature ("the beauty of many hues") is spoken of as an evidence of God's creative power.

words: إِنَّمَا يَخْشَى ٱللَّهَ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ ٱلْعُلَمَٰٓؤُا۟
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True knowledge is spiritual realization that observable phenomena are not all reality and that a realm lies beyond created perception; Asad links this to 2:3, note 3.
rows.anchor: spiritual knowledge, born of the realization that the phenomena which can be observed do not comprise the whole of reality

none: translation only; no separate commentary point
translation only; no separate commentary point
translation only; no separate commentary point

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Urjan is the date-palm raceme; when old and dry it becomes slender and curved like a crescent.
rows.anchor: the meaning of the noun 'urjan - the raceme of the date-palm, which, when old and dry, becomes slender and curves like a crescent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad's gloss of the living as alive of heart signals spiritual responsiveness to the warning.
rows.anchor: warn everyone who is alive [of heart]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This passage resumes the sūra's opening theme of Quranic revelation.
rows.anchor: This passage resumes the theme enunciated in the opening verses of this surah, namely, the revelation of the Qur'an.

rows.speaker: Muhammad's opponents
rows.claim: Muhammad's opponents, both in his time and later, alleged that his claimed revelation was invented as poetry; Asad links this allegation to 26:224.
rows.anchor: the allegation of Muhammad's opponents, in his own as well as in later times, that what he described as divine revelation was in reality

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad distinguishes poetry, where meaning often serves rhythm and melody, from Quranic revelation, where wording, sound, position, rhythm, and melody serve intended meaning.
rows.anchor: whereas in the former the meaning is often subordinated to the rhythm and the melody of language, in the Qur'an the exact opposite is the case

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad's composite rendering of mubin is clear in itself and clearly showing the truth; he refers to 12:2, note 2.
rows.anchor: For this composite rendering of the adjective mubin, see surah 12, note 2.

words: إِنْ هُوَ إِلَّا ذِكْرٌۭ وَقُرْءَانٌۭ مُبِينٌۭ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conjunction wa, as at 15:1, marks the Quran as an integral element in the process of divine revelation.
rows.anchor: with the conjunctive particle wa ("and") being used here, as in 15:1, to point out that the Qur'an is an integral element

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means God's word will come or be proved true against deniers on Judgment Day, as indicated by 36:7.
rows.anchor: Lit., "may come [or "be proved"] true", i.e., on the Day of Judgment

none: translation only; no separate commentary point
translation only; no separate commentary point

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah fled by abandoning his divinely entrusted mission in anger; Asad connects this to the first part of Jonah's story at 21:83.
rows.anchor: when he abandoned the mission with which he had been entrusted by God (see surah 21, note 83, which gives the first part of Jonah's story)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibaq primarily means a slave's running away from his master, explaining the comparison of Jonah's flight to a runaway slave.
rows.anchor: the infinitive noun ibaq (derived from the verb abaqa) denotes "a slave's running- away from his master"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The laden ship alludes to the allegorical center of Jonah's story: a storm threatened the vessel, the sailors cast lots to identify the cause, and Jonah agreed to the procedure.
rows.anchor: The subsequent mention of "the laden ship" alludes to the central, allegorical part of Jonah's story. The ship ran into a storm

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally says Jonah cast lots with the mariner and was among the losers.
rows.anchor: Lit., "he cast lots [with the mariner], and was among the losers".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Biblical account says Jonah admitted fleeing from God and asked to be thrown into the sea so the storm would calm; the sailors complied and the sea ceased raging.
rows.anchor: According to the Biblical account (The Book of Jonah i, 10-l5), Jonah told them that he had "fled from the presence of the Lord"
